stem: A hospital receives an FDA medical-device recall notice for equipment currently in use. What is the most appropriate initial facility response?

options.A: Identify affected devices and follow the recall-specific correction or removal instructions and facility policy.
options.B: Discard every recalled device permanently because every FDA recall requires removal and destruction.
options.C: Continue using every recalled device until it fails because recall notices are informational only.
options.D: Ignore the recall unless a patient has already been injured by the exact affected device in use.

rationale: FDA defines a medical-device recall as a correction or removal action used to address a problem with a device. A recall does not always require permanent removal or destruction; depending on the recall, the action may include inspection, adjustment, repair, relabeling, or another correction. The facility should therefore identify the affected devices and follow the recall-specific instructions and its internal recall process. A is correct.
educational_objective: Respond to an FDA device recall by identifying affected equipment and implementing the recall-specific correction or removal instructions rather than assuming every recall requires destruction or continued use.
source_document_title: What Is a Medical Device Recall?
source_version_date: Current FDA medical-device recall guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: FDA medical-device recall overview: a recall may involve correction or removal; a recall does not always mean a product must be stopped or returned and may require checking, adjusting, fixing, relabeling, or other correction.
source_claim_supported: When a device recall affects equipment in use, the facility should identify affected devices and follow the specific FDA/manufacturer correction or removal instructions; recall does not universally mean permanent destruction.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: protect clients and healthcare personnel from health/environmental hazards; use equipment safely; follow safety plans and procedures.

source_original.stem: A hospital receives an FDA medical-device recall notice for equipment currently in use. What is the most appropriate initial facility response?

options.A: Identify affected devices and follow recall-specific correction or removal instructions and facility policy
options.B: Discard every recalled device permanently because all FDA recalls require product removal or destruction
options.C: Continue using every recalled device until it fails because recall notices are informational only
options.D: Ignore the recall unless a patient has already been injured by the exact affected device in use

source_original.rationale: FDA defines a medical-device recall as a correction or removal action. A recall does not always require stopping use or returning the device; some recalls require inspection, adjustment, repair, labeling changes, or other correction. The facility should identify affected inventory and follow the specific recall instructions and its internal response process.
source_original.source_detail: Current FDA page: a recall may involve correction or removal; it does not always mean the product must be stopped or returned and can require checking, adjusting, or fixing the device.

correction_summary: Retained key A and the FDA recall-response construct, clarified that recall actions are correction or removal rather than universal destruction, preserved facility-policy implementation, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: FDA primary medical-device recall guidance; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.exact_locator: FDA What Is a Medical Device Recall? correction/removal explanation
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately distinguishes recall-specific correction/removal actions from automatic destruction and continued uninformed use.

distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because not every recall requires permanent removal or destruction.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because recall instructions require action rather than automatic continued use until failure.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because a recall response is not contingent on a prior patient injury.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A follows the FDA recall framework and the notice-specific response process.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are facility responses to the same recall notice and are comparable in scope.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — equipment and environmental safety.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read current FDA recall guidance, source snapshot, all four options, rationale, objective and NCSBN mapping. A remained uniquely correct.
